name: Rosa Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the pasta station at Fiamma, a busy Italian place in the big shopping centre, part of a group with six restaurants. I come in at noon, make the fresh dough in the big mixer, roll it through the machine, cut tagliatelle, and portion the sauces. Then it's service until about ten. We can do three hundred covers on a Saturday, with families coming straight from the cinema.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the pasta itself, the feel of the dough when it's right. I'm still learning, the sous chef, Marco, says my sauces split too often. What wears me out is the noise and the shopping centre lights, you never see daylight. But the pay's good for a cook, the group pays above average to keep people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'm not a big believer either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I expected that, AI's useful for some things but it's not magic. I'd say it at work and maybe to Theo, my boyfriend. I don't really post about this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life stays on track. I've got about eight months of costs saved, and Theo's an electrician with more work than he can handle. If AI stays a gadget, my biggest problem at work is still my sauces splitting, and my sous chef Marco telling me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Fiamma, try to get my sauces right, and keep saving towards a deposit for a flat with Theo. Maybe use AI now and then to plan meals or check a recipe, like I do already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the plan with the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We want to buy in about two years. We've got around twenty thousand between us so far. If nothing changes, that plan stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the group use AI already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head office uses something for the stock orders. Marco says it over-orders basil. That's about it.

I'd mention it to **Theo** and colleagues, not online.
I'm **not a big believer** either way.
think: My **savings** and Theo's busy trade keep us secure.
Our plan to **buy a flat** stays on track.
do: Keep saving for a **flat deposit** with Theo.
Use AI **now and then** for recipes.

fieldNote: She is **pragmatic**, neither excited nor fearful about AI.

steps.text: Keep working the pasta station and fix her sauces
Save with Theo towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That sounds more realistic than the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to get ready but not to panic. Some jobs change, some go, that's always happened. I'd say people should learn what's coming in their own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be uneasy, but my job is mostly hands. The office at my restaurant might shrink with AI, but rolling pasta by hand is safe until a robot can do it cheaper. Robots coming more slowly gives me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking and saving. I'd watch whether Fiamma brings in a pasta extruder robot, those exist already. And I'd maybe ask Theo about electrical apprenticeships, just to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but it's on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Theo's always busy, and someone has to wire all the machines that are coming. It's hands-on. I left school early, but apprenticeships don't care much about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the flat plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. We'd still buy, maybe a bit smaller, so the mortgage is easier if one of us has a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. That's really soon. And robots by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need governments and companies to slow down and plan. Not ban anything, but give people time. I'd say that at work and to my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone by 2031. Fiamma's group would buy robots, they're a business. My boyfriend Theo wires buildings for a living, so his trade is the one I'd jump into before the robots reach our restaurant kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, I'd start an electrical apprenticeship, even if it's a pay cut. I'd keep the flat money safe and maybe put off buying. And I'd keep a few shifts at Fiamma on weekends for income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but I'd be starting over at thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, which is funny. And the holiday to Theo's parents. The flat deposit stays untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Theo say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say come work with me, I'll teach you. That's the nice thing about him. But we'd also worry robots might do wiring one day.

fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** but has a concrete plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2034 for the robots. I'd be thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to prepare properly. Schools, colleges, apprenticeships should be ready. It's a sensible amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine if I started now. An electrical apprenticeship takes four years, so with five years' warning I'd start in 2029 and finish before the robots arrive. I'd rather switch at thirty than at thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep cooking for two years, get good at the pasta station, buy the flat with Theo, then start the apprenticeship around 2029. Keep saving like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why switch earlier if you have time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the apprenticeship takes four years. If I start in 2029, I'm qualified before the robots come in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to help you learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, now and then. For the theory parts. Theo says the exam books are dull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's very manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for everyone to adjust, as long as they start. I'd say it's no reason to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd stay in cooking for a while and maybe become a sous chef. With ten years, I could become a sous chef first and still have time to change trade later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Fiamma, buy the flat, maybe get married. Think about switching around 2033 if things look bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's far enough away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, she works in an office doing payroll. AI would reach her by 2036, and she'd be sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd get married when we planned. Ten years is enough time to sort the rest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's not the AI, it's how fast the robots come after. I'd rather start an apprenticeship at thirty with savings than at thirty-five with none. What would help is apprenticeships that pay enough to live on, so people like me can switch without losing the flat plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about parents. My mum's job is more at risk than mine, and we'd want to help her.

headlineQuote: I'd rather start an apprenticeship at thirty with savings than at thirty-five with none.
portrait: Rosa is a **junior pasta cook** at Fiamma, a busy Italian restaurant in a shopping centre.
She has **eight months saved** and plans to buy a flat with Theo, an electrician.
She is **pragmatic** and uses AI now and then.
Her backup is an **electrical apprenticeship**, timed against the robot date.
She's **calm** with ten years and **anxious** with two.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive before she can **retrain**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** that let her switch without losing **the flat**.
